parent.name: Italian Game
parent.overview: White develops the bishop to c4 aiming at f7 and prepares to take the centre with c3 and d4 or, more quietly, d3 (s1, s2). The root is a crossroads: 3...Bc5 (Giuoco Piano) mirrors White's set-up, 3...Nf6 (Two Knights) invites sharper play, and 3...Be7 (Hungarian) is passive and solid (own understanding for the last). Today's main practical line is the Giuoco Pianissimo with c3, d3 and slow manoeuvring, which became fashionable in the 1980s-2000s and again in the 21st century as a way to avoid the Berlin (s1). The older 4.c3 and d4 lines and the Evans Gambit are sharper (s1). It is fundamentally sound with modest winning chances (s1). It is described as accessible to beginners yet used by Giri, So and Vachier-Lagrave (s3).

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Normal Defense
parent.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6
parent.overview: Black answers 3.Nc3 with the natural 3...Nf6, defending d5 and eyeing e4. This is a crossroads in which White chooses between 4.Bg5 (the pin and the classical Orthodox, Lasker, Tartakower and Cambridge Springs lines), 4.cxd5 (the Exchange and Carlsbad structure, dominant at 2500 level) and 4.Nf3, which keeps options open and lets Black pick a QGD, Ragozin (...Bb4) or Semi-Slav (...c6) set-up (s1, s4). The QGD systems are solid with straightforward plans: ...Nf6, ...Be7, ...O-O against most lines, and the ...c5 break (s2). White's typical plans are the minority attack and e4 expansion (s1). The Semi-Slav moves 4.Nf3 c6 5.Bg5 (Botvinnik) are outside the QGD in character, very forcing (s4). The root as a whole is the Orthodox QGD family and its transpositions. The site's current text for this root is a copy of the parent QGD text.

parent.name: French Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...e6 and ...d5, accepting a pawn chain and a space deficit in return for a sound position, and then hits White's pawn centre at its base with ...c5. The fight is over the dark squares d4 and e5. Black's problem piece is the light-squared bishop on c8, hemmed in by the e6 pawn; Black solves it by exchanging it or rerouting it (...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7 with ...Bb5/a4). White typically uses extra space for a kingside attack (f4-f5, and in the Advance the g4/h4 ideas) or expands on the queenside with a3-b4. Play is slower and manoeuvring, with a lot of pawn-break play. It has a reputation for solidity but a cramped early game for Black. The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) is the sharpest branch, the Advance is the main fight in a locked centre, and the Tarrasch, Classical and Exchange are quieter. The root is one position after 1...e6 2.d4 d5; the structures differ strongly by branch.

parent.name: Scandinavian Defense: Modern Variation
parent.overview: Black answers 2.exd5 by developing the knight and delaying the recapture, avoiding the tempo lost when the queen takes on d5. The main line is 3.d4 Nxd5 (the Marshall, as the old name had it), after which 4.Nf3 and 4.c4 Nb6 or ...Bg4 give White a space edge and Black quick development and easy piece play. White can also hold the pawn with 3.c4 (Black strikes back with ...c6 into Panov-type structures, or the Icelandic Gambit 3...e6) or play 3.Bb5+ Bd7. Wikipedia/Emms describe the 2...Nf6 lines as the more tactical branch of the Scandinavian, though sound for Black; White usually keeps a slight initiative through development. Positions are usually open or semi-open with Caro-Kann-like pawn formations (...c6, ...e6) and Black often castles short while White controls more space.

parent.name: Van Geet Opening
parent.overview: White develops a knight to c3, controlling e4 and d5, and keeps the pawn structure undecided to choose a set-up once Black replies. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so Queen's Gambit and English structures are not available without reorganising. Main replies: 1...d5 (the cleanest; 2.e4 transposes to obscure Scandinavian lines, or the Van Geet Attack after 2...d4 3.Nce2), 1...e5 (then 2.e4 Vienna Game, the most common transposition in the database, or 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Napoleon Attack), 1...Nf6 (one of the most unpleasant replies for White) and 1...c5 (transposing to Closed Sicilian or inferior-placed-knight lines). Sources call it sound and low-theory but unambitious: Black equalises with accurate play, so it earns points from surprise rather than from an edge, and masters play it under 1% of the time, though some strong correspondence players use it. The database root has few games itself; most of the subtree (about 290M games) is Vienna, Closed Sicilian and Chigorin-style transpositions that play like those openings.

parent.name: Indian Defense: Anti-Nimzo-Indian
parent.overview: After 3.Nf3 White declines to allow the Nimzo-Indian pin (3.Nc3 Bb4) and leaves the structure open until Black reveals it. Black's reply decides the game: 3...d5 transposes to the Queen's Gambit Declined or the Catalan (the most popular, 40.2 percent at lower ratings and 43.4 percent at 2500), 3...b6 is the Queen's Indian, 3...Bb4+ the Bogo-Indian, and 3...c5 leads to Benoni-style structures (or the Blumenfeld Gambit). Chessiverse calls the move 'slightly more restrained' than 3.Nc3, offering numerous paths to a quiet, positional edge, and a flexible move order rather than a fixed system. Posters on the Chess.com forum point out that 3.Nf3 does not entirely avoid the Nimzo, since 3...Bb4+ 4.Nc3 reaches the Three Knights Nimzo, and that the consensus is that no black reply is worse than equal. White's edge shrinks as ratings rise.

parent.name: Petrov's Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 2.Nf3 by counter-attacking e4 rather than defending e5. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3 both sides have lost an e-pawn and the structure is symmetrical, with the e-file the main open line. Black's aim is to equalise by quick development and piece trades; White tries to turn a small lead in development or slightly freer play into pressure, often castling and using the e-file or a queenside castling and pawn storm. The 3.d4 Steinitz line (3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nxe5 Nd7) and 3.Nc3 (Four Knights transposition) or 3.d3 sidelines give quieter or more varied structures. The main lines are widely played at the top and are known as drawish, though some lines hold real attacking chances for both sides.

parent.name: Philidor Defense
parent.overview: Black defends e5 with the d-pawn instead of the knight, building a compact centre at the cost of space and piece mobility. Wikipedia calls it solid but passive (s1); the dark-squared bishop and sometimes the whole position can be cramped (s2, s4). The usual game is White taking space after 3.d4 or developing with 3.Bc4, and Black setting up the Hanham formation (...Nf6, ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...c6, ...O-O), then freeing the position by ...exd4 or ...d5 at the right moment (s1, s4). Modern analysis finds it dynamically balanced, not just passive (s3). Strong players use it rarely; Wikipedia says no top player used it regularly as of 2017, though it has grown in rapid, blitz and bullet (s1). Move orders matter: Black must avoid several tactical pitfalls (s2, s4).

parent.name: Alekhine Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 Nf6 2. e5 Nd5 3. d4 d6
parent.overview: Black attacks e4 at once with 1...Nf6 and, after 2.e5 Nd5, invites White to build a broad centre with c4, d4 and perhaps f4, planning to attack that centre later with ...d6, ...Nb6, ...Bg4, ...c5 and ...dxe5. White's job is to keep or use the extra space, either with the most ambitious Four Pawns Attack (4.c4 Nb6 5.f4), the popular Modern Variation 4.Nf3, or the less forcing Exchange 5.exd6; 2.Nc3 avoids the main line entirely. Positions lose symmetry from the start and are unbalanced, with a space edge for White against Black's counterplay on the overextended pawns. The opening is regarded as sound, original and tricky but risky (moderate to high), and is only moderately common at the top: Fischer, Korchnoi, Ivanchuk and occasionally Carlsen have played it.
